questions.stem: Money acting as a medium of exchange means that it:
options: is generally accepted in payment for goods and services
allows the value of different goods to be compared
can be held to buy goods and services in the future
is used to record debts that will be paid at a later date
questions.explanation: As a medium of exchange, money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants under barter. Comparing values is its role as a unit of account, and holding it for later is a store of value.

questions.stem: A shop prices a bicycle at $400 and a scooter at $200, so a customer can see the bicycle is worth two scooters. This shows money's function as:
options: a store of value
a standard of deferred payment
a unit of account
a medium of exchange
questions.explanation: A unit of account gives a common measure for comparing the value of different goods. Money is a medium of exchange only when it is actually used to make the purchase.

questions.stem: Why does high inflation weaken money's function as a store of value?
options: Money can no longer be used to compare the prices of different goods
Sellers refuse to accept money and insist on barter instead
Banks stop recording debts in dollars and use foreign currency
Money held today will buy fewer goods and services in the future
questions.explanation: When prices rise quickly, the purchasing power of saved money erodes, so people prefer to hold real assets. Money can still be a unit of account, although frequent price changes make it less convenient.

questions.stem: Which is the main form of money in the Australian economy today, by value?
options: Cheques written by households
Deposits held in bank accounts
Notes and coins in circulation
Gold held by the Reserve Bank
questions.explanation: Most money exists as electronic deposits in bank accounts, transferred by card, online banking and other electronic payments. Notes and coins are a small and falling share of payments.

questions.stem: In the circular flow of income, households:
options: supply factors of production to firms and earn factor incomes
buy factors of production from firms and pay them as wages
collect taxes from firms and provide public goods in return
receive savings from firms and lend them on to the government
questions.explanation: Households own land, labour, capital and enterprise, and earn rent, wages, interest and profit when firms use them. They spend much of this income on firms' output.

questions.stem: The role of the financial sector in the circular flow is to:
options: buy Australian exports and sell imports to Australian households
supply labour to firms in exchange for wages and salaries
channel savings from households into investment by firms
collect taxes and fund public services and transfer payments
questions.explanation: Banks and other intermediaries take in savings and lend them to borrowers, turning a leakage into an injection. Taxes and public services belong to the government sector.

questions.stem: Which flow is an injection into the five-sector circular flow of income?
options: Household spending on imported goods
Money deposited in household savings accounts
Export revenue earned by Australian firms
Income tax paid by Australian households
questions.explanation: Injections, investment, government spending and exports, add spending to the flow from outside the household and firm sectors. Taxes, imports and savings are leakages.

questions.stem: Which list contains only leakages from the circular flow?
options: Savings, taxation and imports
Investment, government spending and exports
Savings, government spending and exports
Consumption, investment and imports
questions.explanation: Leakages are income not spent on domestic output: saving, paying tax and buying imports. Investment, government spending and exports are the injections that match them.

questions.stem: An Australian household buys a television made in South Korea. In the circular flow, this spending is:
options: neither, as only spending by firms enters the model
a leakage, as income flows to the international sector
an injection, as spending flows from the international sector
an injection, as household consumption on goods rises
questions.explanation: Spending on imports leaves the domestic flow and becomes income for overseas producers. Exports are the matching injection, where foreign spending enters the Australian flow.

questions.stem: In an economy, savings are $80b, taxation $120b and imports $100b, while investment is $90b, government spending $110b and exports $70b. The level of national income will tend to:
options: rise, because leakages exceed injections
rise, because injections exceed leakages
stay the same, because the economy is in equilibrium
fall, because leakages exceed injections
questions.explanation: Leakages total 80 + 120 + 100 = $300b and injections 90 + 110 + 70 = $270b. With more income leaving than entering, spending and income contract until the two are equal.

questions.stem: The circular flow model is in equilibrium when:
options: savings equal government spending
exports equal taxation revenue
household income equals business revenue
total leakages equal total injections
questions.explanation: When S + T + M = I + G + X, the amount leaving the flow is matched by the amount entering it, so national income is stable. Individual leakages need not equal individual injections.

questions.stem: Business confidence collapses and firms cut planned investment by $20 billion, with no other change. In the circular flow model the most likely result is:
options: national income rises, since firms now have more funds available to save
national income is unchanged, as investment is a leakage, not an injection
national income falls by more than $20 billion as cuts in spending flow on
national income falls by exactly $20 billion and then immediately recovers
questions.explanation: Lower investment reduces income for those who would have supplied the projects, who then spend less in turn, so income falls by a multiple of the initial cut. Investment is an injection.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the level of economic activity in the circular flow?
options: A rise in government spending on new roads
A rise in the share of income households save
A rise in household spending on imported goods
A rise in income tax rates paid by households
questions.explanation: Government spending is an injection, so it adds to total spending and income. Higher saving, imports and taxes are all leakages, which reduce spending on domestic output.

questions.stem: Households decide to save a larger share of their incomes, and the financial sector lends all of the extra savings to firms for investment. The effect on national income is most likely to be:
options: roughly neutral, as the extra leakage is matched by an extra injection
a large fall, as saving is always a leakage that is never returned
a large rise, as both saving and investment add to national income
a large fall, as investment is a leakage when it is funded by savings
questions.explanation: If the financial sector channels all new saving into investment, the injection offsets the leakage and the flow is maintained. Income falls only if the extra saving is not borrowed and spent.

questions.stem: Gross domestic product (GDP) measures:
options: the total value of all goods and services sold by a country to other countries
the total income earned by a country's citizens, wherever they are working
the value of all goods, including intermediate goods, produced in a country
the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country
questions.explanation: GDP counts final output produced within Australia's borders over a year or quarter. Counting intermediate goods would double count, and exports are only one part of GDP.

questions.stem: GDP includes the contributions of both the private and public sectors. Which is a public sector contribution to GDP?
options: A listed mining company exporting iron ore overseas
A household paying a private builder to renovate
A state government building a new public hospital
A family-owned bakery selling bread to its customers
questions.explanation: Output produced or purchased by governments, such as hospitals, schools and roads, is the public sector's contribution. Production by private businesses for sale is the private sector's contribution.

questions.stem: Using the expenditure approach, GDP is calculated as:
options: wages + rent + interest + profit - government spending
investment + government spending + exports - consumption
consumption + investment + government spending + exports - imports
consumption + savings + taxation + exports + imports
questions.explanation: Total spending on Australian output is C + I + G + (X - M). Imports are subtracted because they are produced overseas, even though they are included in spending.

questions.stem: Which is a reason why economies pursue higher GDP?
options: Higher output automatically shares income equally among households
Higher output always reduces pollution and environmental damage
Higher output removes the problem of scarcity for every household
Higher output can raise material living standards and create jobs
questions.explanation: Growth in GDP provides more goods and services, more employment and more tax revenue to fund services. It does not guarantee equality or a better environment, and scarcity always remains.

questions.stem: In economics, the term business cycle describes:
options: the flow of income between households and businesses each year
fluctuations in the level of economic activity over time
the steady long-run growth of an economy's potential output
the movement of a product through its sales life from launch
questions.explanation: Economic activity rises and falls around its long-run trend in expansions and contractions. The flow of income between sectors is the circular flow model.

questions.stem: The highest point of economic activity, just before a downturn begins, is the:
options: contraction
peak
trough
expansion
questions.explanation: At the peak the economy is operating at or above capacity and growth begins to slow. The trough is the lowest point, after which a recovery begins.

questions.stem: During the expansion phase of the business cycle, the economy usually experiences:
options: unchanged output with sharply rising unemployment
rising output and employment, with inflationary pressure building
falling output and employment, with inflationary pressure easing
falling output but rising employment as firms hire more workers
questions.explanation: In an upturn spending, production and hiring increase, and as spare capacity is used up prices tend to rise faster. Falling output and easing inflation describe a contraction.

questions.stem: Which combination of conditions is most typical at the trough of the business cycle?
options: high unemployment and rising inflation
high unemployment and low inflation
low unemployment and high inflation
low unemployment and low inflation
questions.explanation: The trough follows a contraction, when weak spending leaves many workers unemployed and firms with spare capacity, so price pressures are low. Low unemployment with high inflation is typical near a peak.

questions.stem: Data show real GDP growth slowing from 4% to 1%, unemployment rising from 4.2% to 5.0% and inflation easing. The economy is most likely in:
options: an expansion, recovering from a trough
a contraction, after passing a peak
an expansion, approaching a peak
a trough, at the start of a recovery
questions.explanation: Slowing growth, rising unemployment and easing inflation are signs of a downturn after a peak. A recovery from a trough would show growth picking up and unemployment starting to fall.

questions.stem: Which event is most likely to start a downturn in the Australian business cycle?
options: A cut in interest rates that lowers the cost of borrowing
A recession among Australia's major trading partners
A large rise in world prices for Australia's exports
A rise in consumer confidence and household spending
questions.explanation: A global recession reduces demand for Australian exports and confidence, lowering spending and output. The other options would all add to spending and activity.

questions.stem: Changes in consumer and business confidence can cause fluctuations in the business cycle because:
options: confidence affects how much households spend and firms invest
confidence determines the level of taxation set by government
confidence fixes the exchange rate between the dollar and other currencies
confidence controls the number of people of working age
questions.explanation: Optimism encourages spending and investment, while pessimism leads people to delay purchases and projects, so shifts in confidence can amplify the cycle. Tax rates are set by government policy.

questions.stem: An economist says a boom 'contains the seeds of its own downturn'. Which chain of events best illustrates this?
options: Weak demand lowers inflation, interest rates fall and spending then rises
Strong demand lowers unemployment, so wages fall and spending then rises
Weak demand raises unemployment, so firms invest more and output rises
Strong demand raises inflation, interest rates rise and spending then slows
questions.explanation: As a boom stretches capacity, inflation rises; higher interest rates and costs then dampen spending, turning the expansion into a contraction. The weak-demand chain describes a recovery, not the end of a boom.

questions.stem: How does a contraction in the business cycle usually affect households?
options: Higher inflation increases the real value of savings
Job losses and fewer hours cut incomes and confidence
Rising wages and overtime increase incomes and spending
Falling unemployment raises household bargaining power
questions.explanation: In a downturn firms cut staff and hours, so household incomes fall and job insecurity rises. Rising wages and low unemployment are features of an expansion.

questions.stem: During an expansion, businesses are most likely to experience:
options: large amounts of unused productive capacity and stock
rising sales and profits, and difficulty finding skilled workers
falling sales and profits, and many unemployed workers to choose from
falling costs of labour and materials as demand weakens
questions.explanation: Strong demand lifts sales and profits, but as the labour market tightens firms find it harder to hire and costs rise. Spare capacity and cheap labour are features of a downturn.

questions.stem: During a contraction, the government's budget position usually worsens even without any change in policy. This is because:
options: the Reserve Bank must transfer its reserves to the government
the government must repay all of its debt during a contraction
tax revenue falls and spending on unemployment benefits rises
tax revenue rises and spending on unemployment benefits falls
questions.explanation: Lower incomes and profits reduce tax collections, while more people claim payments such as JobSeeker, so the budget moves towards deficit automatically. These automatic stabilisers cushion the downturn.

questions.stem: A long period of strong expansion is most likely to create which problem for the economy?
options: Deflation as businesses compete for scarce customers
Rising inflation as demand outstrips productive capacity
Rising unemployment as firms cut production and staff
Falling government revenue as incomes and profits fall
questions.explanation: When spending grows faster than the economy can produce, shortages of labour and materials push up prices. Rising unemployment and falling revenue are problems of a contraction.

questions.stem: A recession is commonly defined in Australia as:
options: one year in which unemployment rises above 5%
two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth
two consecutive quarters of positive real GDP growth
one quarter in which the inflation rate exceeds 3%
questions.explanation: This rule of thumb is a technical recession; a fall in output alongside sharply rising unemployment confirms it. A depression is a far deeper and longer downturn.

questions.stem: Which correctly lists the four stages of the business cycle in order, starting from the peak?
options: peak, contraction, expansion, trough
peak, contraction, trough, expansion
peak, trough, contraction, expansion
peak, expansion, trough, contraction
questions.explanation: After the peak, activity contracts to a trough, then expands to the next peak. A trough cannot be followed by a contraction, because it is the lowest point.

questions.stem: In the circular flow model, the government sector affects the level of economic activity by:
options: collecting savings, which are an injection, and lending, which is a leakage
buying imports, which are an injection, and selling exports, a leakage
setting interest rates, which directly fix the level of household income
collecting taxes, which are a leakage, and spending, which is an injection
questions.explanation: Taxation removes income from the flow, while government spending on goods, services and transfers adds to it. Interest rates are set by the Reserve Bank, part of the financial sector, not by the Budget.

questions.stem: The government raises taxes by $10 billion and increases spending by $10 billion. In the circular flow model, the most likely immediate effect is that:
options: leakages and injections both rise by $10 billion, so their balance is unchanged
leakages rise by $20 billion, so national income must fall sharply
injections rise by $20 billion, so national income must rise sharply
only leakages change, because government spending is not part of the model
questions.explanation: Higher taxes add $10 billion to leakages and higher spending adds $10 billion to injections, leaving the balance between them unchanged. In more detailed models the effect is slightly expansionary, because some of the tax would otherwise have been saved.

questions.stem: The international sector in the circular flow model includes:
options: spending on exports and imports between Australia and other countries
spending by state and local governments on infrastructure
savings held by households in Australian banks and super funds
wages paid by Australian firms to their Australian employees
questions.explanation: Exports bring foreign spending into the Australian flow and imports send spending overseas. Government infrastructure spending belongs to the government sector, and savings to the financial sector.

questions.stem: Quarterly real GDP growth in a year was +0.6%, -0.2%, +0.3% and -0.4%. Did the economy enter a technical recession during that year?
options: No, because real GDP grew strongly in the first quarter of the year
No, because there were no two consecutive quarters of negative growth
Yes, because real GDP fell in two of the four quarters in the year
Yes, because growth over the year was well below its long-run trend
questions.explanation: A technical recession needs two negative quarters in a row; here each fall was followed or preceded by growth. Weak growth and two scattered negative quarters signal a soft economy, but not a technical recession.

questions.stem: Which combination of changes is most likely to cause national income to rise?
options: Imports rise and business investment falls
Households save less and exports rise
Households save more and exports fall
Taxes rise and government spending falls
questions.explanation: Less saving reduces leakages and higher exports increase injections, so spending in the flow rises. Each other combination raises leakages or lowers injections, or both.

questions.stem: Output starts to grow again after a trough, but the unemployment rate keeps rising for several more months. The most likely reason is that:
options: the labour force shrinks as soon as output begins to grow again
inflation rises sharply at the trough, forcing firms to cut jobs
firms wait until they are confident the recovery will last before hiring
firms hire many new workers as soon as output reaches the trough
questions.explanation: Employment tends to lag output: firms first use existing staff more fully and add hours before taking on new workers. Unemployment can also rise as discouraged workers rejoin the labour force to look for jobs.
